provenance.method: lesson notes written from the NERDC 2025 scheme of work outline; every week keeps its scheme topic and bullets as the teaching spine

topics.title: Revision of sss two work
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to recall key concepts from SSS 2 Further Mathematics.
The students should be able to solve basic problems from previous topics.

Introduction:
We have covered fundamental topics in SSS 2 that form the basis for SSS 3 work.
Today we will refresh our memory through a pure math warm up and quiz.

Content:
Pure math warm up involves solving algebraic equations, calculus problems, and geometry questions from SSS 2 curriculum. The quiz will cover topics like differentiation, integration, circle geometry, and vectors. Each student will attempt 10 questions from past WAEC questions within 20 minutes.

Class activity:
Students will work in pairs to solve selected problems from the quiz, discussing their approaches and solutions.

Evaluation questions:
1. Differentiate x^3 + 2x^2 - 5x + 3 with respect to x.
2. Find the integral of 4x^2 + 3x - 2.
3. Prove that the angle subtended by an arc at the center is twice the angle subtended at the circumference.
4. Solve the simultaneous equations: 2x + y = 10 and x - y = 2.

Summary:
Today's revision session has refreshed our understanding of key SSS 2 Further Mathematics concepts.

topics.title: Sets and functions
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to define domain and range of functions.
The students should be able to determine domain and range given different functions.
The students should be able to solve exam questions on domain and range.

Introduction:
We have previously studied basic set theory and functions in SSS 2.
Today we will build on that knowledge by examining domain and range in more detail.

Content:
The domain of a function is the set of all possible input values (x-values) for which the function is defined. The range is the set of all possible output values (y-values). For example, the function f(x) = 1/(x-2) has a domain of all real numbers except x=2. In Nigeria, we can think of domain as the different markets in Lagos where you can buy kerosene, while range represents the possible prices you might find.

Class activity:
Students will be given various functions and asked to determine their domains and ranges, then present their findings to the class.

Evaluation questions:
1. Define domain and range of a function.
2. Find the domain and range of f(x) = √(x-3).
3. Determine the domain and range of g(x) = 1/(x+4).
4. Solve: If f(x) = 2x+1 and the domain is {0,1,2,3}, find the range.

Summary:
Understanding domain and range is crucial for analyzing functions in Further Mathematics.

topics.title: Polynomials
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to state the factor theorem.
The students should be able to apply the factor theorem to find roots of polynomials.
The students should be able to solve exam questions on polynomials.

Introduction:
We have studied basic operations on polynomials in previous classes.
Today we will examine the roots and factor theorem which are essential for solving polynomial equations.

Content:
The factor theorem states that if f(x) is a polynomial and f(a) = 0, then (x-a) is a factor of f(x). For example, if f(x) = x^3 - 6x^2 + 11x - 6 and f(1) = 0, then (x-1) is a factor. We can use this to factorize polynomials completely. In Nigeria, we can think of this like finding the root causes of a problem before addressing the symptoms.

Class activity:
Students will work in groups to factorize given polynomials using the factor theorem and then solve the resulting equations.

Evaluation questions:
1. State the factor theorem.
2. Use the factor theorem to factorize x^3 - 2x^2 - 5x + 6.
3. Find all roots of the polynomial 2x^3 - 3x^2 - 11x + 6.
4. If (x-2) is a factor of x^3 + ax^2 + bx - 10 and f(1) = -4, find a and b.

Summary:
The factor theorem provides a powerful method for solving polynomial equations by identifying factors.

topics.title: Binomial series
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to state the binomial theorem for positive integer exponents.
The students should be able to expand expressions using the binomial series.
The students should be able to solve exam questions on binomial expansions.

Introduction:
We have previously studied basic binomial expansions in SSS 2.
Today we will expand our knowledge to handle more complex binomial series expansions.

Content:
The binomial theorem states that (a + b)^n = Σ(nCr) × a^(n-r) × b^r for r = 0 to n, where nCr is the binomial coefficient. For example, (x + 2)^4 = x^4 + 4x^3(2) + 6x^2(2)^2 + 4x(2)^3 + (2)^4 = x^4 + 8x^3 + 24x^2 + 32x + 16. In Nigeria, we can think of this like expanding the different ways to share items among people, similar to how market traders might distribute goods among customers.

Class activity:
Students will practice expanding various binomial expressions using the binomial theorem, including those with fractional and negative exponents.

Evaluation questions:
1. State the binomial theorem for positive integer exponents.
2. Expand (2x - 3y)^4 using the binomial theorem.
3. Find the coefficient of x^3 in the expansion of (1 + 2x)^5.
4. Expand (1 - x/2)^6 up to the term in x^3.

Summary:
The binomial theorem provides a systematic method for expanding expressions of the form (a + b)^n.

topics.title: Trigonometric identities
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to prove trigonometric identities.
The students should be able to solve trigonometric equations.
The students should be able to solve exam questions on trigonometric identities.

Introduction:
We have studied basic trigonometric ratios and identities in previous classes.
Today we will examine more complex proofs and equations involving trigonometric identities.

Content:
Trigonometric identities are equations that are true for all values of the variables. Common identities include sin²θ + cos²θ = 1, 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ, and sin(A±B) = sinAcosB ± cosAsinB. To prove identities, we typically work with one side to transform it into the other side. For example, to prove (1 + cosθ)(1 - cosθ) = sin²θ, we expand the left side to get 1 - cos²θ, which equals sin²θ by the Pythagorean identity. In Nigeria, we can think of these identities like the consistent patterns in the harmattan season that occur year after year.

Class activity:
Students will work in pairs to prove given trigonometric identities and solve equations using these identities.

Evaluation questions:
1. Prove that (1 + tanθ)(1 - tanθ) = 1 - tan²θ.
2. Solve the equation 2sin²θ + 3cosθ = 0 for 0° ≤ θ ≤ 360°.
3. Prove that sin(A+B) + sin(A-B) = 2sinAcosB.
4. If sinθ = 3/5 and θ is acute, find the value of cos2θ.

Summary:
Mastering trigonometric identities is essential for solving complex trigonometric equations and problems.

topics.title: Sequences and series
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to define arithmetic and geometric progressions.
The students should be able to find the nth term and sum of AP and GP.
The students should be able to solve exam questions on sequences and series.

Introduction:
We have previously studied basic sequences and series in SSS 2.
Today we will examine more advanced concepts in arithmetic and geometric progressions.

Content:
An arithmetic progression (AP) is a sequence where each term differs from the previous by a constant difference d. The nth term is a + (n-1)d and the sum of n terms is n/2[2a + (n-1)d]. A geometric progression (GP) is a sequence where each term is obtained by multiplying the previous term by a constant ratio r. The nth term is ar^(n-1) and the sum of n terms is a(r^n - 1)/(r - 1) for r ≠ 1. For example, the prices of goods in a Nigerian market might form an AP with constant inflation, while the population growth might form a GP.

Class activity:
Students will solve problems involving finding terms and sums of APs and GPs, including those requiring the formation and solution of equations.

Evaluation questions:
1. Define arithmetic and geometric progressions.
2. The 3rd term of an AP is 11 and the 7th term is 23. Find the 10th term.
3. Find the sum of the first 8 terms of the GP 3, 6, 12, 24, ...
4. A man saves ₦1000 in the first month and increases his savings by ₦200 each subsequent month. How much will he have saved after 12 months?

Summary:
Sequences and series provide mathematical models for many real-world situations involving patterns and growth.

topics.title: Matrices
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to perform basic operations on matrices.
The students should be able to find the inverse of a 2x2 matrix.
The students should be able to solve exam questions on matrices.

Introduction:
We have previously studied basic matrix concepts in SSS 2.
Today we will examine matrix operations and the process of finding matrix inverses.

Content:
Matrices are rectangular arrays of numbers arranged in rows and columns. Basic operations include addition, subtraction, and scalar multiplication. For matrix multiplication, the number of columns in the first matrix must equal the number of rows in the second matrix. The inverse of a 2x2 matrix [a b; c d] is (1/det)[d -b; -c a], where det = ad - bc is the determinant. For example, the inverse of [2 3; 1 4] is (1/5)[4 -3; -1 2]. In Nigeria, we can think of matrices like the seating arrangements in a danfo bus, where each person has a specific position.

Class activity:
Students will perform operations on given matrices and find inverses of 2x2 matrices, then use these to solve simple systems of equations.

Evaluation questions:
1. Define a matrix and state the conditions for matrix multiplication.
2. If A = [1 2; 3 4] and B = [2 0; 1 3], find AB.
3. Find the inverse of the matrix [3 1; 5 2].
4. Use matrix method to solve the system: 2x + 3y = 7, x - y = 1.

Summary:
Matrix operations and inverses provide powerful tools for solving systems of linear equations.

topics.title: Determinants
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to calculate the determinant of a 2x2 and 3x3 matrix.
The students should be able to use determinants to solve systems of equations.
The students should be able to solve exam questions on determinants.

Introduction:
We have previously studied matrices in the previous lesson.
Today we will examine determinants and their application in solving systems of equations.

Content:
The determinant of a 2x2 matrix [a b; c d] is calculated as ad - bc. For a 3x3 matrix [a b c; d e f; g h i], the determinant is a(ei - fh) - b(di - fg) + c(dh - eg). Determinants can be used to solve systems of linear equations using Cramer's rule, which states that for a system Ax = B, x_i = det(A_i)/det(A), where A_i is the matrix formed by replacing the ith column of A with B. For example, to solve 2x + 3y = 7 and x - y = 1, we find det(A) = -5, det(A_1) = -10, and det(A_2) = -5, giving x = 2 and y = 1.

Class activity:
Students will calculate determinants of given matrices and use them to solve systems of linear equations.

Evaluation questions:
1. Calculate the determinant of the matrix [2 3; 1 4].
2. Find the determinant of [1 2 3; 4 5 6; 7 8 9].
3. Use determinants to solve the system: 3x + 2y = 8, x - y = 1.
4. If det(A) = 0 for a system of equations, what does this imply about the solution?

Summary:
Determinants provide a systematic method for solving systems of linear equations and determining the nature of their solutions.

topics.title: Complex numbers
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to represent complex numbers on an Argand diagram.
The students should be able to perform operations on complex numbers.
The students should be able to solve exam questions on complex numbers.

Introduction:
We have previously studied basic number systems in mathematics.
Today we will extend our knowledge to include complex numbers and their graphical representation.

Content:
Complex numbers are numbers of the form a + bi, where a and b are real numbers and i is the imaginary unit with i² = -1. An Argand diagram is a graphical representation of complex numbers where the real part is plotted on the x-axis and the imaginary part on the y-axis. Operations on complex numbers include addition (a+bi) + (c+di) = (a+c) + (b+d)i, subtraction (a+bi) - (c+di) = (a-c) + (b-d)i, and multiplication (a+bi)(c+di) = (ac-bd) + (ad+bc)i. For example, the complex number 3 + 4i is represented as the point (3,4) on an Argand diagram. In Nigeria, we can think of complex numbers like the combination of physical goods and services in our economy.

Class activity:
Students will plot complex numbers on Argand diagrams and perform operations on given complex numbers, then verify their results graphically.

Evaluation questions:
1. Define a complex number and explain how it is represented on an Argand diagram.
2. Plot the complex numbers 2 + 3i and -1 + 2i on an Argand diagram.
3. If z1 = 3 - 2i and z2 = 1 + 4i, find z1 + z2 and z1 × z2.
4. Express the complex number (1 + 2i)/(3 - i) in the form a + bi.

Summary:
Complex numbers extend the real number system and provide solutions to equations that have no real solutions.

topics.title: Revision and exam practice
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to apply knowledge from the term to solve exam questions.
The students should be able to identify areas of weakness for further study.
The students should be able to improve their exam technique and time management.

Introduction:
We have covered various topics in Further Mathematics this term.
Today we will practice past paper questions to prepare for the end-of-term examination.

Content:
The revision session will focus on past WAEC Further Mathematics Paper 1 questions covering all topics studied this term. Students will work individually to complete a timed test of selected questions from past papers. After completion, we will mark and correct the papers together, discussing common mistakes and effective problem-solving strategies. For example, when solving matrix problems, we'll emphasize the importance of careful calculation and verification of results.

Class activity:
Students will complete a timed test of past paper questions, then participate in a group discussion to review solutions and address any difficulties encountered.

Evaluation questions:
1. Solve the system of equations using matrices: 2x + y = 7, 3x - 2y = 4.
2. Find the domain and range of f(x) = √(4 - x²).
3. Prove that cos3θ = 4cos³θ - 3cosθ.
4. Expand (1 - 2x)^6 up to the term in x³.
5. If the 3rd term of a GP is 18 and the 5th term is 162, find the first term and the common ratio.

Summary:
Today's revision session has helped consolidate our understanding of Further Mathematics topics and improved our exam technique.
